growth_story.headline: Ecuador's oil-boom gains stalled after 2015: despite a 2025 rebound, income per person is about where it first was in 2014.
growth_story.arc: From 1990 to 2000 income per person grew just 0.2 percent a year, and the decade ended in a banking collapse: income per person fell 6.4 percent in 1999, and Ecuador adopted the US dollar in January 2000. From 2001 to 2014 growth picked up to 3.1 percent a year, carried in its later years by record oil prices that paid for a large rise in public spending and investment. When oil prices fell after 2014, growth slowed to 0.3 percent a year over 2015 to 2025, and to 0.4 over the last decade against 2.7 in the decade before. Government debt rose, the pandemic cut income per person by 10.3 percent in 2020, and droughts that disrupted power and worsening insecurity added to the strain in 2024, when it fell 2.8 percent. A 2.9 percent rebound in 2025, under an IMF-supported program, brought income per person back to its 2023 peak, about where it first stood in 2014.

threads.text: In the late 1990s low oil prices and crop failures from El Nino hit the economy, leading banks were shut down and deposits were frozen in March 1999. Ecuador answered by adopting the US dollar in January 2000, and with other crisis measures this brought inflation down.

threads.title: Oil boom, then oil bust
threads.text: Record oil prices lifted growth and public revenue until 2014 and paid for more social programs and public investment. When prices fell, growth stalled in 2015 and turned negative in 2016, deficits widened and government debt climbed.

growth_story.tension: The IMF and World Bank describe a strong rebound in 2025 and growth that keeps beating forecasts. In the data, the 2025 gain only brought income per person back to its 2023 peak, about where it first stood in 2014. Part of the gap is that the sources track total output, which grows faster than income per person while the population keeps growing.
